meta.title: Use of Laboratory Sink with Eye Wash in Pharmaceutical Chemistry Laboratory

sections.purpose: To provide immediate emergency ocular and facial decontamination following accidental exposure to chemical reagents, solvents, or corrosive substances in the Pharmaceutical Chemistry laboratory.
sections.scope: Applicable to Pharmaceutical Chemistry laboratory as a mandatory emergency first-aid facility for chemical splashes, and for routine glassware and equipment washing.
procedure: In case of chemical splash to the eyes or face: act immediately without hesitation — time to initial flushing is critical.
Guide the affected person to the eye wash station without delay.
Activate the eye wash (push handle or pedal) — water should flow from both nozzles simultaneously.
The affected person should hold eyelids open using fingers, and position eyes directly over the nozzle stream.
Flush continuously for a minimum of 15 minutes for all chemical exposures.
For acid exposure: flush for 15 minutes minimum; then proceed to medical evaluation.
For alkali (base) exposure: flush for 20–30 minutes — alkalis penetrate deeper and require extended flushing.
For organic solvent splash: flush for 15 minutes; solvent in eyes causes chemical burns and corneal damage.
Have another person call emergency medical services immediately while flushing continues.
Do not stop flushing to look for damage — 15 minutes is the minimum regardless of apparent severity.
After flushing, transport immediately to ophthalmology or emergency medical facility.
For routine washing: scrub glassware with detergent and bottle brushes; rinse 3× with tap water then 2× with distilled water.
Log weekly eye wash activation tests (10–15 second flush) in the safety equipment register.
precautions: Test the eye wash weekly — inactive eye wash nozzles become colonized with bacteria that cause additional injury.
Keep the area in front of the eye wash completely unobstructed at all times.
Never wear contact lenses when handling strong acids, bases, or organic solvents — lenses trap chemicals and increase damage.
Mark the eye wash location with clearly visible signage.
All staff must receive eye wash training during laboratory induction.
Do not use eye wash for draining organic solvents — segregate chemical waste properly.
